กำเนิดอักษร · Where the alphabet came from

The Thai script descends from Brahmi (India, 3rd c. BCE) through the Pallava script of South India, carried across the Bay of Bengal with Sanskrit, then through Old Khmer — the script of Angkor, whose empire ruled the Chao Phraya basin before the Tai states rose.

Tradition credits King Ram Khamhaeng of Sukhothai, 1283, with reshaping Khmer letters into ลายสือไทย 'Thai writing'. (The famous Inscription One that tells this story has itself been the subject of a long authenticity controversy — know the debate exists.) Two genuine innovations stand out: vowels written on the main line, and the world's first tone marks — no earlier script anywhere marked tone.

Why 44 consonants for ~21 consonant sounds? Because the alphabet kept the entire Sanskrit varga grid — the voiced, voiceless, aspirated, and retroflex distinctions of Indic — even where Thai never pronounced them apart. Those "redundant" letters are the etymological tracer-dyes of rule K1. Two letters (ฃ ฅ) have died; the rest soldier on.

Then came the Great Tone Split (roughly 15th–17th c.): Thai devoiced its voiced consonants, and the old voicing contrast was reborn as tone differences. The three consonant "classes" of modern Thai are fossilized voicing: high class = old voiceless aspirates & fricatives, mid = old plain voiceless, low = old voiced. The tone rules feel arbitrary until you know this — then they are just the ghost of a sound change.

ผังวรรค · The varga grid

Thai alphabetical order IS Sanskrit phonological order: each row (วรรค) is one place of articulation — unvoiced, unvoiced-aspirate, voiced, voiced-aspirate, nasal. Color = tone class: high · mid · low.

velarกขคฆง

dentalตถทธน
pphbbhm
labialปผพภม

Then the sonorants ย ร ล ว, the three s's ศ ษ ส (Skt. ś ṣ s — all now /s/), ห, ฬ (Skt./P. ḷ), อ. Reading a loanword's spelling against this grid IS reading its Sanskrit.

ผังวรรณยุกต์ · Tone chart

Tone = initial's class × syllable type × tone mark. Live = ends in vowel/sonorant; dead = ends in -k -t -p or short vowel. IPA tone letters here: ˧ mid · ˨˩ low · ˥˩ falling · ˦˥ high · ˩˥ rising.

classlivedead+ ่+ ้+ ๊+ ๋
mid ก จ ด ต บ ป อmidlowlowfallinghighrising
high ข ฉ ถ ผ ฝ ศ ส หrisinglowlowfalling——
low ค ช ท พ ฟ ม น ร ลmidshort: high
long: falling		fallinghigh——

ห leading a low sonorant (หน หม หล) lends its high class; อ does the same for mid (อย่า อยู่ อย่าง อยาก). This chart is rule K11's engine.

RTGS does not mark tone or vowel length — it is a locator system. The IPA toggle and 🔊 buttons carry what it drops. Search is tone- and aspiration-insensitive, so panya, punya, and bhanya all reach ปัญญา — it matches on the consonant skeleton, the same trick Wehr's root order plays on Arabic.

วันนี้ · Today

รากศัพท์ — a root dictionary of Thai

Ordinary dictionaries sort words A–Z, so ปัญญา, วิญญาณ, and สัญญา live pages apart. This one sorts by root: all three sit under √jñā "know", and you learn the system, not just the words — the way the classic Hans Wehr dictionary organized Arabic.

Reading an entry

Families show derivatives with strict RTGS (toggle IPA for tones, 🔊 to hear), source forms in Pali/Sanskrit, and frequency dots — ●●● everyday, ●● common, ● bookish. K-chips (K2, K4…) name the sound-change rule that mangled the word; tap to read it. Confidence tags say how far to trust each etymology: verified cross-checked, standard mainstream but unchecked, debated genuinely contested.

The daily loop

วันนี้ gives you one root each morning to carry. Spot a family member in the wild — a sign, a menu, a sermon — and log it with 👁. Sightings become flashcards that return on schedule. The margin notes write the book.

About · วิธีทำ

Method

Root families are editorially assembled: an Indic root or a native head morpheme, then the Thai words that derive from it, glossed and annotated. Assignments follow standard Indological practice (Pali/Sanskrit verbal roots as given in the Pali Text Society and Monier-Williams traditions). Where a derivation is contested or the Thai word's route in is disputed, it is tagged debated rather than smoothed over.

Every derivative carries a confidence tag and source codes. verified means the etymology was cross-checked against Thai Wiktionary's independent entry and agreed. standard means it is the mainstream assignment but has not been checked against a second source in this edition. debated means sources disagree or the derivation is traditional rather than demonstrated. CUR = editorial, WIKT = corroborated by Thai Wiktionary.

Known limits

Romanization and IPA are machine-generated (tltk) and contain occasional errors on rare compounds. Frequency tiers come from the Thai National Corpus and reflect written Thai. The candidate list is machine-clustered and unedited by design. Thai-language rule translations have not had a native editorial pass. None of this is a substitute for the Royal Institute Dictionary as the authority on modern Thai.

Sources

Royal Institute Dictionary (พจนานุกรมฉบับราชบัณฑิตยสถาน) · Pali Text Society Pali–English Dictionary (Rhys Davids & Stede) · Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit–English Dictionary · Thai Wiktionary via kaikki.org wiktextract (CC BY-SA 3.0) · Thai National Corpus (Chulalongkorn) for frequency · PyThaiNLP and tltk for segmentation, romanization, and IPA · Haas, Thai-English Student's Dictionary (1964) for the compound-nesting principle · Wehr, A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic, for the whole idea.

Licence

Editorial content and code: free and open, reusable with attribution. The Wiktionary-derived layer (whole-word glosses, candidate list, extended families) is CC BY-SA 3.0 and carries that obligation with it — attribute Thai Wiktionary and keep derivatives share-alike. The two layers are kept structurally separate in the data files so the obligation stays scoped.
